name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
description: People continue investing in a losing course of action because of what they've already invested, even when that prior investment is irrecoverable and irrelevant to the rational forward-looking decision.
design_relevance_note: Invoked (and sometimes deliberately exploited in dark-pattern design) to justify progress-loss warnings ('you'll lose your progress') that pressure continued engagement.
prevalence_note: One of the most mainstream, widely-known cognitive biases outside of academia entirely, not just within design practice.

findings.description: Across several experiments, people were more likely to continue investing in a failing course of action once they had already committed prior, non-recoverable resources to it, even when continuing was economically irrational — the definitive early experimental demonstration of the sunk cost effect.
findings.source_venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

findings.description: Directly re-testing the classic Arkes & Blumer (1985) sunk-cost vignettes (N = 395, two experiments), internal consistency across the standard vignette set was consistently poor (ω = 0.14-0.57), with only weak correlations even between highly similar scenarios — meaning these widely-used vignettes likely don't measure one single 'sunk cost bias' construct, but several distinct psychological processes (loss aversion, commitment consistency, social signaling) bundled under one popular label.
findings.source_title: On the Low Reliability of Sunk Cost Vignettes

applications.title: Duolingo's 'Investment Wager' streak bet
applications.description: Duolingo lets users wager 50 in-game gems on completing a 7-day streak, timed to appear right after a reward moment -- once staked, users have a sunk investment in the outcome that Growth.Design frames as increasing their likelihood of continuing to engage rather than losing the wager.
applications.ethical_note: This deliberately engineers a sunk-cost pressure -- staking in-game currency specifically to make quitting feel like a loss -- rather than relying on a naturally-occurring commitment. The currency at stake (gems) is low-value/virtual, which keeps real-world harm low, but the mechanism itself is a deliberate behavioral lever, not an incidental side effect, which is why this isn't graded user_beneficial despite the harmless stakes.

applications.title: The Concorde: continuing a commercially doomed project because of how much had already been invested
applications.description: The Concorde supersonic airliner project was predicted to be a commercial failure early in its development, but the British and French governments and manufacturers continued the joint venture to completion anyway -- so strongly associated with escalation of commitment driven by sunk costs that the sunk cost fallacy is sometimes called the 'Concorde fallacy' after this specific case.
applications.ethical_note: A large-scale historical illustration of sunk-cost-driven decision-making at the organizational/government level, not a designed influence on an individual user -- relevant to product and engineering leadership decisions (continuing a failing project or feature because of prior investment) as much as to end-user-facing design patterns like Duolingo's own streak-investment mechanic.
